nameStory: The name 'field marigold' comes from this cheerful flower's preference for open fields and disturbed ground, combined with its bright golden blooms that resemble the more familiar garden marigolds. The genus name Calendula comes from the Latin word for 'little calendar,' referring to how these flowers seem to bloom throughout much of the growing season.
description: Field marigold is a small annual or biennial herb that grows 4 to 20 inches tall with bright yellow to yellow-orange daisy-like flowers. This European native has slender, hairy stems topped with single flower heads that can reach up to 4 centimeters wide. The plant has a delicate, somewhat weedy appearance but makes up for its modest size with cheerful, sunny blooms that stand out against its lance-shaped leaves.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Single bright yellow to yellow-orange flower heads up to 1.5 inches wide, with cheerful ray petals surrounding a center of tiny yellow disc florets, blooming one per stem tip

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves that feel slightly fuzzy and are attached to the stem by short leaf stalks (petioles), giving them a neat, orderly appearance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing plant 4-20 inches tall with slender stems covered in soft hairs that you can feel when you gently run your finger along them

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces unusual curved or ring-shaped seeds (achenes) that come in three different forms, helping the plant spread in various ways

habitat: Field marigold is extremely rare in New England, found occasionally in disturbed soils, waste places, and agricultural edges. When it does appear, look for it in sunny, open areas with well-drained soil, often near human activity like roadsides or old farmland.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with fuzzy lance-shaped leaves, beginning their growth cycle in disturbed soil.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with bright yellow-orange flower heads opening in sunny weather, most visible and identifiable during this time.
seasonality.fall: Late flowers may still be blooming while earlier ones have gone to seed, producing the distinctive curved achenes for next year's plants.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants have died back completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to sprout the following growing season.

funFact: Field marigold produces three completely different seed shapes from the same flower head - some curved like tiny bananas, others ring-shaped like miniature donuts, and still others boat-shaped - each designed to travel and disperse in different ways!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other small yellow composite flowers, but the combination of single flower heads per stem, lance-shaped leaves on petioles, and fuzzy stems helps distinguish it from similar species like hawkweeds or wild mustards.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, field marigold is not closely related to the common garden marigolds (Tagetes) that many people know - those are actually from Mexico and belong to a different genus entirely, though both are in the large daisy family.
compareHints: Field marigold differs from its more common relative, pot marigold (Calendula officinalis), by being smaller overall with more delicate stems and smaller flower heads. Pot marigold is typically more robust, often grown in gardens, and has larger, showier orange or yellow blooms that can reach 2-4 inches across compared to field marigold's more modest 1.5-inch flowers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Field marigold (Calendula arvensis), the only other Calendula species you might encounter, has much smaller, paler yellow flowers and grows as a weedy annual in agricultural areas.
